## Frequently asked questions

## ### What is the Digital Omnibus on AI?


The Digital Omnibus on AI is Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, an amending act that entered into force on 27 July 2026 and changed Regulation (EU) 2024/1689: the EU AI Act. It deferred the high-risk compliance deadlines, added two prohibited practices, softened the AI literacy duty, gave the AI Office direct enforcement powers, and clarified how penalties apply to SMEs.

## ### Did the Digital Omnibus delay the EU AI Act?


It delayed part of it. The high-risk obligations moved: Annex III use cases from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and Annex I product-safety systems from 2 August 2027 to 2 August 2028. Nothing already in force was rolled back: the prohibitions, the AI literacy duty, the general-purpose AI model obligations and the Article 50 transparency rules all continue to apply, and the Omnibus added two new prohibitions.

## ### How many prohibited AI practices are there now?


Ten. Eight have been unlawful since 2 February 2025. The Digital Omnibus inserted Article 5(1)(ba) on non-consensual intimate imagery and Article 5(1)(bb) on child sexual abuse material, both applying from 2 December 2026. Material that still refers to eight prohibitions is describing the superseded text.

## ### When do high-risk AI obligations apply after the Omnibus?


2 December 2027 for AI systems in the eight Annex III use-case areas, and 2 August 2028 for AI systems that are safety components of products covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation. Both dates are later than the adopted text provided.

## ### What changed about AI literacy under Article 4?


The duty was softened from ensuring a sufficient level of AI literacy to taking measures to support it. It still applies to every provider and deployer regardless of risk tier and has done since 2 February 2025, but compliance is now assessed on the measures taken rather than the level of literacy achieved.

**6.1. AI Regulatory Sandboxes**

Articles 57–59 provide controlled AI regulatory sandboxes for developing, testing and validating innovative AI systems under competent national-authority supervision before market placement. The Digital Omnibus on AI permits an EU-level sandbox coordinated by the AI Office and extends access beyond small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups to small mid-cap companies (SMCs).

The Digital Omnibus on AI also postpones the deadline for establishing at least one national AI regulatory sandbox from 2 August 2026 to 2 August 2027, a full year later. These changes foster innovation and facilitate business compliance before the high-risk rules fully apply.

**The “Digital Omnibus on AI” Regulation introduces crucial AI Act amendments by postponing application of the high-risk AI rules and more broadly simplifying its administrative framework.**

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council, adopted on 8 July 2026 (“Digital Omnibus on AI” or “Regulation”), was published in the Official Journal of the European Union on 24 July 2026.

The Digital Omnibus on AI forms part of the EU’s Omnibus legislative packages to reduce administrative burdens and enhance competitiveness. It accompanies the forthcoming “Digital Omnibus” Regulation amending the GDPR, ePrivacy, the Data Act and other Acts.

The Digital Omnibus on AI introduces targeted amendments and simplifications to the AI Act, without, however, changing its structure and risk-based approach. Given the imminence of the 2 August 2026 deadline for the application of high-risk AI systems’ provisions, the Digital Omnibus on AI entered into force only three days after publication, on 27 July 2026, rather than after the standard twenty-day period.

The most significant amendments of the Digital Omnibus on AI concern:

The Digital Omnibus on AI amends the AI Act’s implementation timeline, principally by postponing the rules governing high-risk AI systems. Article 6 sets the classification rules for systems qualifying as high-risk. The original dates were 2 August 2026 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems under Article 6(2) and Annex III, and 2 August 2027 for high-risk systems embedded as safety components under Article 6(1) and Annex I. Delayed standards, common specifications, alternative guidance and the establishment of national competent authorities would have made those dates disproportionately costly. The Digital Omnibus on AI therefore postpones the date on which the high-risk AI obligations become applicable to two new dates:

Article 50 of the AI Act lays down transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems. The Digital Omnibus on AI introduces no new transparency obligations and does not substantively alter the existing requirements, which continue to include informing users when they interact with an AI system, labelling AI-generated or AI-manipulated content, and disclosing the use of emotion-recognition systems or synthetic content (deepfakes).

The key change concerns the application date of the Article 50(2) provider duty to apply machine-readable marking to AI-generated or manipulated content, including synthetic and manipulated audiovisual material (deepfakes).

The key change concerns the application date of the Article 50(2) provider duty to apply machine-readable marking to AI-generated or manipulated content, including synthetic and manipulated audiovisual material (deepfakes).

New Article 111(4) of the AI Act, inserted by the Digital Omnibus on AI, requires providers of systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026 (the four-month transition under Recital 38). This grace period applies only to those existing systems. Systems placed on the market after 2 August 2026 must comply upon placement because Article 50’s general application date remains 2 August 2026 under Article 113, as amended.

Under the AI Act’s risk-based classification, Article 5 designates certain practices as prohibited because they are considered dangerous to fundamental rights, democracy or human dignity that they are banned outright in the EU.

The Digital Omnibus on AI amends Article 5 by adding the following two categories to the prohibited practices already in place:

The Regulation differentiates the prohibition for providers from that for deployers. Providers may not place systems on the market where designed for such purposes, or where reasonably and foreseeably usable for them without adequate technical safeguards. Deployers may not use systems to create or manipulate such material.

Both new prohibitions take effect for providers and deployers from 2 December 2026. The existing prohibited practices under Article 5 have been in force since 2 February 2025.

The Digital Omnibus on AI narrows the definition of “safety component” in Article 3(14), which informs high-risk classification. Under new Article 6(1a), AI systems used solely for non-safety-related user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control are not safety components and therefore are not high-risk on that basis. Under new Article 6(1b), however, systems whose failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety remain safety components. This keeps classification aligned with the AI Act’s risk-based approach.

Article 4 required providers and deployers to take measures, to the greatest extent possible, to ensure adequate “AI literacy” among staff and others operating or using AI systems on their behalf. The duty covered appropriate knowledge, skills and understanding of AI capabilities, risks and potential effects, taking account of the technical background, experience and role of the persons concerned.

## Did the Digital Omnibus delay the EU AI Act?

It delayed part of it, and expanded another part. The high-risk obligations moved out by 16 months for Annex III use cases and 12 months for Annex I products. Nothing already in force was rolled back, and two new prohibited practices were added, taking the Article 5 list from eight to ten.

That combination is why “the AI Act was delayed” is a misleading summary. An organisation reading it that way risks missing two bans that bite on 2 December 2026 and a marking deadline on the same date.

## Which deadlines moved

Two high-risk deadlines in Article 113 were deferred, and one date was created that does not appear in the adopted text at all.

## What this means for compliance work

The deferral buys time on the heaviest workstream and buys none at all on the nearest deadline.

- **Do not stand down high-risk work.** Conformity assessment for an Annex III system is a multi-quarter programme. December 2027 is a schedule change, not a reprieve.
- **Check exposure to the two new prohibitions before December 2026.** They apply in the €35 million / 7% tier, the same as the original eight.
- **Confirm synthetic-content marking on legacy systems.** Generative systems already on the market must carry machine-readable marking by 2 December 2026 under Article 50(2).
- **Revisit AI literacy evidence.** The duty is now about measures rather than outcomes, which changes what you should be recording, not whether you owe it.
- **Re-check any guidance dated before 27 July 2026.** Deadlines, prohibition counts and penalty mechanics in older material are likely to be wrong.

## Frequently asked questions

## ### What is the Digital Omnibus on AI?


The Digital Omnibus on AI is Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, an amending act that entered into force on 27 July 2026 and changed Regulation (EU) 2024/1689: the EU AI Act. It deferred the high-risk compliance deadlines, added two prohibited practices, softened the AI literacy duty, gave the AI Office direct enforcement powers, and clarified how penalties apply to SMEs.

## ### Did the Digital Omnibus delay the EU AI Act?


It delayed part of it. The high-risk obligations moved: Annex III use cases from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and Annex I product-safety systems from 2 August 2027 to 2 August 2028. Nothing already in force was rolled back: the prohibitions, the AI literacy duty, the general-purpose AI model obligations and the Article 50 transparency rules all continue to apply, and the Omnibus added two new prohibitions.

## ### How many prohibited AI practices are there now?


Ten. Eight have been unlawful since 2 February 2025. The Digital Omnibus inserted Article 5(1)(ba) on non-consensual intimate imagery and Article 5(1)(bb) on child sexual abuse material, both applying from 2 December 2026. Material that still refers to eight prohibitions is describing the superseded text.

## ### When do high-risk AI obligations apply after the Omnibus?


2 December 2027 for AI systems in the eight Annex III use-case areas, and 2 August 2028 for AI systems that are safety components of products covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation. Both dates are later than the adopted text provided.

## ### What changed about AI literacy under Article 4?


The duty was softened from ensuring a sufficient level of AI literacy to taking measures to support it. It still applies to every provider and deployer regardless of risk tier and has done since 2 February 2025, but compliance is now assessed on the measures taken rather than the level of literacy achieved.

**The “Digital Omnibus on AI” Regulation introduces crucial AI Act amendments by postponing application of the high-risk AI rules and more broadly simplifying its administrative framework.**

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council, adopted on 8 July 2026 (“Digital Omnibus on AI” or “Regulation”), was published in the Official Journal of the European Union on 24 July 2026.

The Digital Omnibus on AI forms part of the EU’s Omnibus legislative packages to reduce administrative burdens and enhance competitiveness. It accompanies the forthcoming “Digital Omnibus” Regulation amending the GDPR, ePrivacy, the Data Act and other Acts.

The Digital Omnibus on AI introduces targeted amendments and simplifications to the AI Act, without, however, changing its structure and risk-based approach. Given the imminence of the 2 August 2026 deadline for the application of high-risk AI systems’ provisions, the Digital Omnibus on AI entered into force only three days after publication, on 27 July 2026, rather than after the standard twenty-day period.

The most significant amendments of the Digital Omnibus on AI concern:

The Digital Omnibus on AI amends the AI Act’s implementation timeline, principally by postponing the rules governing high-risk AI systems. Article 6 sets the classification rules for systems qualifying as high-risk. The original dates were 2 August 2026 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems under Article 6(2) and Annex III, and 2 August 2027 for high-risk systems embedded as safety components under Article 6(1) and Annex I. Delayed standards, common specifications, alternative guidance and the establishment of national competent authorities would have made those dates disproportionately costly. The Digital Omnibus on AI therefore postpones the date on which the high-risk AI obligations become applicable to two new dates:

Article 50 of the AI Act lays down transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems. The Digital Omnibus on AI introduces no new transparency obligations and does not substantively alter the existing requirements, which continue to include informing users when they interact with an AI system, labelling AI-generated or AI-manipulated content, and disclosing the use of emotion-recognition systems or synthetic content (deepfakes).

New Article 111(4) of the AI Act, inserted by the Digital Omnibus on AI, requires providers of systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026 (the four-month transition under Recital 38). This grace period applies only to those existing systems. Systems placed on the market after 2 August 2026 must comply upon placement because Article 50’s general application date remains 2 August 2026 under Article 113, as amended.

Under the AI Act’s risk-based classification, Article 5 designates certain practices as prohibited because they are considered dangerous to fundamental rights, democracy or human dignity that they are banned outright in the EU.

The Digital Omnibus on AI amends Article 5 by adding the following two categories to the prohibited practices already in place:

The Regulation differentiates the prohibition for providers from that for deployers. Providers may not place systems on the market where designed for such purposes, or where reasonably and foreseeably usable for them without adequate technical safeguards. Deployers may not use systems to create or manipulate such material.

Both new prohibitions take effect for providers and deployers from 2 December 2026. The existing prohibited practices under Article 5 have been in force since 2 February 2025.

The Digital Omnibus on AI narrows the definition of “safety component” in Article 3(14), which informs high-risk classification. Under new Article 6(1a), AI systems used solely for non-safety-related user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation, convenience or quality control are not safety components and therefore are not high-risk on that basis. Under new Article 6(1b), however, systems whose failure or malfunctioning would endanger health and safety remain safety components. This keeps classification aligned with the AI Act’s risk-based approach.

Article 4 required providers and deployers to take measures, to the greatest extent possible, to ensure adequate “AI literacy” among staff and others operating or using AI systems on their behalf. The duty covered appropriate knowledge, skills and understanding of AI capabilities, risks and potential effects, taking account of the technical background, experience and role of the persons concerned.

## What this means for compliance work

The deferral buys time on the heaviest workstream and buys none at all on the nearest deadline.

- **Do not stand down high-risk work.** Conformity assessment for an Annex III system is a multi-quarter programme. December 2027 is a schedule change, not a reprieve.
- **Check exposure to the two new prohibitions before December 2026.** They apply in the €35 million / 7% tier, the same as the original eight.
- **Confirm synthetic-content marking on legacy systems.** Generative systems already on the market must carry machine-readable marking by 2 December 2026 under Article 50(2).
- **Revisit AI literacy evidence.** The duty is now about measures rather than outcomes, which changes what you should be recording, not whether you owe it.
- **Re-check any guidance dated before 27 July 2026.** Deadlines, prohibition counts and penalty mechanics in older material are likely to be wrong.

For high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(1), that Regulation applies in conjunction with the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I. In certain cases, it is possible for such Union harmonisation legislation to lay down requirements that achieve the same or a higher level of protection of relevant public interests as achieved by the specific requirements or obligations laid down in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. In that case, it should be possible to limit the application of specific requirements or obligations laid down in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 in order to facilitate compliance, minimise administrative burden and duplications, while preserving the level of protection ensured by that Regulation. Such limitation should be possible where, and to the extent that, the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I lays down requirements providing for an equivalent level of protection of health, safety or fundamental rights as the requirement or obligation concerned. The Commission should be empowered to adopt delegated acts to supplement that Regulation by identifying such cases and specifying the products concerned, the requirements or obligations that may be limited, and the conditions and scope of any limitation, ensuring that the level of protection provided by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is not reduced.
